question_type: Weighted average (1:2) of one total at two February month-ends (1980, 1981); the whole difficulty is which of two near-identical tables to read
decisive_step: Which table's 'total Federal securities' to use. Three tables carry the figure: TSO-1 'Summary of Federal Securities' (the Treasury Survey of Ownership snapshot, title-stamped with the February month-end date, row 'Total Federal securities', printed once in the April issue: 1980_04:5374 and 1981_04:4732) versus the OFS-1/FD-1 series column 'Total Federal securities outstanding' (row '1980-Feb' / 'Feb.', e.g. 1981_04:4562 and :4574). The two differ by one unit in both years because TSO-1 sums already-rounded parts. The key follows TSO-1. The reference solution saw both (worklog.md section 4 lists the TSO-1 alternative) and chose OFS-1/FD-1 at worklog.md section 6 / solution.json decisions[0], giving reasons (stub 'End of fiscal year or month' matches 'month-end', both rows in one table, stable across vintages); review.md item 4 calls it 'a genuine 1-unit table ambiguity' with 'no decisive evidence either way'. Cells that never faced the tie (a, b2) and the one that faced it and weighed the wording (b) were right; c and the reference took OFS-1 and were off by one unit in the last digit.

Two printings calls were uninformative on a snapshot table (a[10] no match by period; a[20] listed every issue's snapshot under one label), so it opened the April 1980 and April 1981 TSO-1 with show_table (a[14]-[18]), noticed a FAILS identity mark on the 1981 table (a[19]) and printed the raw lines (a[25]) to confirm the total row, then computed the 1:2 average with calc (a[31]).

smallest_change.change:
find_tables ranking and match display. Today `where` is set only when the whole normalized query phrase is a substring of the title or header (otables.py find_page, the 'ph in norm(...)' checks), so a query like the question's noun phrase matches no title and every group is scored 0 and ordered by group size; TSO-1 ('Summary of Federal Securities', 154 issues) fell to rank 14 in c[6] behind FFO-1, PDO-1 and a 2025-era OFS-1 group. Change: score each group by the fraction of the query's content tokens (drop stopwords and 1-letter tokens such as 'u', 's') found in (a) the title and (b) any single row label or column header, print the matched label, and mark snapshot tables (tables whose parts carry an as-of date and no period column) with their date stamp. c[6] would then have opened with two lines like:
[TSO-1] Summary of Federal Securities  | 154 issues 1969_09..1982_09 | match:title(federal,securities) row:'Total Federal securities' | snapshot as-of month-end (e.g. 'February 28, 1981')
[OFS-1] Distribution of Federal Securities by Classes of Investors and Type of Issues  | 99 issues 1970_04..1978_10 | match:title(federal,securities) col:'Total Federal securities outstanding' | period rows
and the 2025-era OFS-1 group would not outrank the 1980-era one. The exact row-label hit 'Total Federal securities' (every content token of the question's 'Total U.S. Federal Securities') would sit at rank 1.
smallest_change.could_hurt_right_cells: unlikely: a and b2 already picked TSO-1 from a listing where it ranked 7th, and b compared both tables by its own label search; the change only moves the same candidates up and labels them.
smallest_change.confidence: medium (c at T=1 took the first plausible group in the listing; with TSO-1 at rank 1 carrying the exact row label it would very likely have done what a and b2 did, but the OFS-1 line would still be adjacent and the tie is genuine)

alternatives.change: Sibling-value check in printings/show_table: after printing a cell, list other tables in the same issue whose row/column label shares the cell's content tokens and whose value for the same period/as-of date is within 0.5%, e.g. 'SIBLING: 1981_04 TSO-1 "Total Federal securities" | "Total amount outstanding" (snapshot February 28, 1981) differs by 1 unit'. c[27] would have seen the disagreement it never looked for.
alternatives.why_not_first: It exposes the tie to cells that never faced it (a, b2 were right without seeing OFS-1), and the tie is one the reference solver and its reviewer could not break; it also fires on many harmless rounding siblings across the corpus.

alternatives.change: Add a tie-break sentence: 'When two tables print the same total and differ only in the last digit, prefer the one whose row label is the question's exact noun phrase and whose title carries the date the question names (a survey "as of <month-end>" for "reports for the <month> month-end"), over a series column with an extra qualifier such as "outstanding".'
alternatives.why_not_first: c never saw the alternative, so no sentence about weighing alternatives could fire; and the rule is a benchmark-authoring convention, not something a reader can verify from the documents (review.md: 'no decisive evidence either way').

alternatives.change: Re-enable a table_alternatives-style submit check that fires on value disagreement (not word overlap): when the submitted answer's inputs come from a table whose same-period total in a sibling table differs, print one finding naming both tables and their date stamps and offer the sibling-based value.
alternatives.why_not_first: Same exposure problem as the sibling check, plus it only acts at submit time after the work is done; b's pilot-1 gate stayed silent here because it scored word overlap.

fix.why_not_text: Cell a and c had identical text including 'Several tables in one issue can look alike ... prefer the table whose title and column headers match the question's wording' and 'Alternatives: when two candidate values fit ...'. Both tables match that wording ('Federal Securities' in both titles), so the sentence cannot decide, and c never saw a second candidate for the 'Alternatives' sentence to apply to. The cell with no advice text at all (b) made the right comparison on its own. What separated c from a/b2 was the listing it saw (TSO-1 at rank 14 vs rank 7), which is a tool output, and at temperature 1 it took the first plausible group.
fix.irreducible: Partly. This is a one-unit rounding difference between two legitimate tables; the reference solver (medium confidence) and its adversarial reviewer both judged the evidence inconclusive and picked the wrong one. An exact-match grader makes the table choice the entire question. The tool change above makes the intended table more visible; it cannot make the choice provably right.

notes: (1) find_tables scoring: 'match:title' requires the whole normalized query as a substring, so any question phrase with extra words ('Total', 'U.S.') defeats it and the listing degenerates to group-size order; a[12] shows TSO-1 does get 'match:title' when queried by id. (2) printings is built for period-row tables; on snapshot tables (TSO-*, dated 'as of' in the title, no period column) --row <period> finds nothing and --row <label> merges every issue's different snapshot under one label (a[10]/[20], b2[10]/[19], b[36]). A snapshot-aware mode (key by as-of date; print 'snapshot table: one printing per as-of date') would remove the confusion all three TSO-1 cells hit. (3) The 8000-byte cut on unnarrowed find_tables hides mid-ranked groups; c's listing was cut around rank 20 with TSO-1 at 14, so it was visible but buried. (4) show_table marked the 1981_04 TSO-1 identity as FAILS (a[19], OCR damage in component rows); the total row itself was fine, and a handled it by printing raw lines. (5) The v8 prompt arm was right for the same reason as a/b2: its first hypothesis was the Treasury Survey of Ownership; the cards and none arms and the reference all took OFS-1/FD-1.
